articles.title: When London Bridge was rebuilt in Arizona, workers numbered its individual granite stones before dismantling it; decades later, visitors can still spot some of those markings on the historic structure
articles.summary: London’s famous bridge across the Thames river has suffered many travesties: it has fallen down time and time again, but still stood strong throughout.
articles.body: London’s famous bridge across the Thames river has suffered many travesties: it has fallen down time and time again, but still stood strong throughout.The bridge that kept falling downCirca AD 50-1176, several wooden iterations of the London Bridge were built again and again, only to fall due to storm, fire or ice damage. Then came the Old London Bridge, built in 1209 under the direction of Peter de Colechurch. The stone bridge was lined with houses and stood for more than 600 years, till an unfortunate fire took it out. The bridge’s history has been anything but a smooth crossing.In 1831, it was eventually replaced by the New London Bridge. Designed by Scottish engineer John Rennie the Elder, its construction began in 1824, and the bridge officially opened on August 1, 1831. The bridge was built from granite and was supported by nearly 2000 timber pilings, a substantial feat at the time. In 1896 the bridge was the busiest point in London, and one of its most congested; 8,000 pedestrians and 900 vehicles crossed every hour.But, the automobile finally caught up with the London Bridge. The 1,000-foot span had stood for over 130 years and survived strafing during World War II’s London Blitz, but it was unequipped for modern traffic and was slowly sinking into the River Thames at a rate of one inch every 8 years. A bridge built for horse-drawn carriages was now expected to accommodate the motor age. Renovations were deemed impractical, so the City of London resolved to build a wider, more car-friendly replacement. A new concrete-and-steel bridge was subsequently constructed between 1967 and 1972, opening in March 1973.A bridge for sale, anyone?With a replacement underway, the City of London had to decide what to do with the old granite bridge. Instead of sending the entire structure to the scrapyard, an unconventional suggestion emerged: why not sell it?City councillor Ivan Luckin was instrumental in convincing his colleagues that the bridge could find a buyer in the United States. In 1968, he travelled to America to market it as a historic monument rather than simply an outdated piece of infrastructure. One city's infrastructure problem was about to become another city's biggest selling point. His pitch rested on the fact that London had been home to a river crossing at the site since Roman times. After arriving in America, Luckin promoted it as a timeless landmark, an heir to 2,000 years of history going back to the 1st century A.D., to the time of the Roman Londinium.The London Bridge sales pitch raised more than a few eyebrows in the United States, but for one businessman, it seemed like a natural fit. Robert McCulloch was a Missouri-born industrialist who had made millions heading up companies that sold oil, motors and chainsaws. Shamelessly eccentric, the tycoon also had a penchant for pursuing pie-in-the-sky business schemes.The tall story of a transatlantic crossingRobert Paxton McCulloch was already a multi-millionaire by the time he turned 18. But inheriting part of his grandfather’s fortune in 1925 didn’t blunt his ambition or work ethic. Driven by a compulsion to invent, after graduating from Stanford University he started a company that created supercharged car engines.When his business associate C.V. Wood told him about London Bridge, the two concluded that it was just the kind of eye-catching centerpiece Lake Havasu needed. McCulloch even hatched a plan to carve one of the lake’s peninsulas into an island so the bridge would have something to span.Negotiations for the purchase proceeded rapidly during the spring of 1968. According to McCulloch, the most difficult part was hashing out a sales price with the City of London authorities. Finally, after learning that dismantling the bridge would cost London $1.2 million, McCulloch and Wood decided to offer double that amount. As a sweetener, McCulloch tacked on an additional $60,000: $1,000 for each year old he would be when the bridge reopened at Lake Havasu. In April 1968, for a final price of $2,460,000, Robert McCulloch became the proud owner of the world’s largest antique.The world's biggest jigsaw puzzleThus, began the journey of solving the world’s biggest jigsaw puzzle. The original granite structure was taken apart piece by piece. Before dismantling, its 10,276 exterior granite blocks were numbered to make reconstruction possible.The markings were not random. Each stone received a four-number identification system. The first number indicated the arch span to which it belonged, the second identified its row, and the final two specified its position within that row. This meant that workers in Arizona could identify precisely where each individual piece belonged when putting the bridge back together. In fact, visitors can still spot some of these markings on the granite today.Across the ocean, the stones went on a little cruise vacation of their own. They were packed and shipped by sea through the Panama Canal to Long Beach, California. From there, trucks transported them across the American desert to Lake Havasu City. The first truckload arrived on 9 July 1968. The reconstruction was supervised by architect Robert Beresford, who worked with copies of Rennie's original plans. A crew of approximately 40 workers undertook the reassembly over the next 3 years.But, how could this bridge now carry the load of Arizonian traffic? Here is where the engineers showed off their cleverness. The original bridge was not simply rebuilt as a solid structure of granite. Workers constructed a hollow core of steel-reinforced concrete and used the original granite as its exterior facing. This made the reconstructed bridge lighter and stronger, allowing it to accommodate modern vehicular traffic.McCulloch also needed the bridge to span water in its new home. The structure was reconstructed across a peninsula, after which workers excavated a channel through the land and allowed water to flow beneath it. This turned the peninsula into an island and gave the bridge an actual crossing to perform. A bridge that had spent over a century in London was now getting an entirely new lease of life in the desert.The shipping, assembly and excavation of the channel reportedly cost approximately $7 million, over and above the purchase price. It was quite possibly the most expensive jigsaw puzzle ever assembled.A London Bridge Arizona-boundThe sweet Brit found itself a new home in the sun-soaked Arizona desert, trading the chilly waters of the Thames for the warmer shores of Lake Havasu. One can only hope it has adjusted to the change in weather. Even decades later now, visitors can still spot some of those markings of the original numbering on the historic structure.As the hit song by Bread put it back in 1969, “London bridge is finally fallin' down, They packed it up and shipped it outta town”. This is one fall people are surprisingly happy about.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: $445m down the drain? Elon Musk's Republican gamble fails; 'guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work'
articles.summary: Tech billionaire Elon Musk's record-breaking $445 million bet on Republican candidates has failed to deliver the political victories he hoped for.
articles.body: Tech billionaire Elon Musk's record-breaking $445 million bet on Republican candidates has failed to deliver the political victories he hoped for. Several of his preferred candidates suffered defeats in the US mid-term elections.From Texas to Ohio, the results dealt a major blow to Musk's political influence, while a surprise Democratic victory in Texas also raised questions over his ambitious plans to expand data centre operations in the state.Musk, who emerged as one of the biggest losers of election night, spent an estimated $445 million backing Republican candidates and causes. More than $200 million went towards Texas-related efforts alone. His spending made him the largest individual political donor in modern US history and set a record for money spent by a non-candidate during an election cycle. Yet, the candidates he supported were defeated across several key contests.The defeats included Ken Paxton's Senate race in Texas and Vivek Ramaswamy's bid for governor in Ohio. The biggest setback for Musk, however, could be in Texas, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa secured a surprise victory over incumbent Republican Greg Abbott in the gubernatorial race.The result has implications beyond Musk's political investments. Texas had emerged as a major destination for companies seeking to build data centres and expand artificial intelligence infrastructure. The state was seen as a favourable environment for such projects at a time when communities across the US were increasingly resisting large data centre developments over concerns about their impact.Musk's companies have significant ambitions in the state. Hinojosa's victory could now introduce uncertainty over the political and regulatory environment surrounding future data centre projects."Amid data center backlash all across the country, Texas was supposed to be an AI oasis, where people would be able to build data centers no matter what was happening in the rest of America," Politico reported quoting Sam Koppelman, the publisher of Hunterbrook Media, an investigative journalism outlet connected to a hedge fund, "This election totally changed that."Musk responds with 'space lasers' jibeAs the Republican losses became clear, Musk turned to sarcasm on X early Wednesday. The billionaire, who had spent hundreds of millions of dollars backing candidates, appeared to poke fun at the election outcome and the criticism surrounding his political involvement."Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time 🤷‍♂️," Musk posted shortly before 1.15am ET.He followed it with another remark that appeared to reference the Democratic victory in Texas and the uncertainty surrounding his data centre plans."Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," he wrote.The posts came after an election in which Musk's financial backing failed to translate into victories for several of the Republican candidates he supported. His comments also brought attention to the potential business implications of the results, particularly in Texas.Democratic Congress could spell more trouble for MuskMusk could face another challenge as Democrats are expected to take control of both chambers of Congress, potentially with comfortable majorities. The shift in power could give them greater scope to scrutinise the influence of wealthy technology executives and their financial involvement in political campaigns.Musk has been a prominent Republican donor and an outspoken supporter of candidates aligned with the party. His record-breaking election spending could make him a particular focus for Democrats, who have argued that technology billionaires wield disproportionate influence over American politics.Representative Greg Casar, a Democrat from Texas, said voters had rejected Republican candidates partly because of their association with wealthy AI investors."Voters rejected Republicans in part because they were bought and paid for by AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement on Tuesday evening, as per a report by Politico."Democrats must hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."The comments signal the possibility of a more confrontational relationship between Musk and a Democratic-controlled Congress. With Democrats expected to take over key leadership positions in both chambers, scrutiny of the political influence and spending of major technology executives could intensify.You use AI every day. articles.title: Did Vivek Ramaswamy 'shoot himself in the foot'? Why Ohio may have rejected him
articles.summary: Vivek Ramaswamy's defeat in Ohio's gubernatorial election was a major setback for a Republican candidate who had Donald Trump's endorsement, substantial
articles.body: Vivek Ramaswamy's defeat in Ohio's gubernatorial election was a major setback for a Republican candidate who had Donald Trump's endorsement, substantial financial backing and national name recognition. Democrat Amy Acton defeated the biotech entrepreneur to become Ohio's first Democratic governor in 20 years and the first woman elected to the office.A campaign too closely tied to TrumpRamaswamy's association with Trump was initially an advantage. The President endorsed him early, and vice president JD Vance, an Ohio native, campaigned for him. But that alliance became a potential liability as voters expressed concerns about the administration's economic record and the cost of living.Acton's campaign sought to portray Ramaswamy as a wealthy outsider disconnected from the financial pressures facing ordinary Ohioans, including the effects of tariffs and rising fuel prices.The result was especially striking in a state Trump had won in the previous three presidential elections. Ramaswamy's defeat suggests that presidential backing and national prominence were not enough to overcome the local concerns shaping the governor's race.The attack ad that backfiredOne of the campaign's most damaging controversies involved an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who called her daughter a liar and urged voters not to elect her. The ad drew condemnation from Democrats and Republicans because of the sensitive circumstances surrounding Acton's childhood and her long estrangement from her mother.Acton had spoken about experiencing childhood abuse and homelessness. Her stepfather was indicted over sexual abuse allegations involving her, and her mother subsequently lost custody of her children. The advertisement brought renewed attention to these painful experiences and prompted criticism that the campaign had crossed a line.Ramaswamy defended the ad as a legitimate challenge to Acton's credibility, with Trump and Vance also backing him. But the controversy widened divisions among Republicans and drew criticism from prominent Ohio figures, including outgoing governor Mike DeWine, who called for the advertisement to be removed while maintaining his endorsement of Ramaswamy. The ad was eventually pulled from the air about a week before Election Day.The episode reinforced Acton's effort to present herself as a candidate focused on public service rather than personal attacks. While it is impossible to establish how many votes the controversy cost Ramaswamy, it became a defining moment in the final stretch of the campaign.Acton focused on affordability and healthcare Acton's campaign offered a contrasting message. A physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, she became widely known during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic, when she worked alongside Republican governor Mike DeWine. Although her pandemic record became a target for conservative criticism, she used her public-health experience to establish her credentials on healthcare.She also drew on her personal background, speaking about childhood hardship, including periods of homelessness. Her emphasis on affordability, access to healthcare and public education gave voters a policy-focused alternative to Ramaswamy's promises of deregulation and conservative reforms.Acton also had an advantage in her familiarity with Ohio. Her career in state government and her experience during the pandemic gave her an established profile, even though she had never held elected office. Ramaswamy, despite being a Cincinnati native, faced criticism that his wealth and national political ambitions made him an outsider to the concerns of middle-class voters.A costly campaign with limitsRamaswamy and his allies spent more than $100 million on the race, substantially outspending Acton's campaign. Yet the financial advantage did not translate into victory. The campaign also faced tensions within Republican ranks: primary challenger Casey Putsch attracted nearly 18% of the Republican primary vote, and later said he planned to vote for Acton.The outcome suggests that campaign spending, endorsements and national visibility cannot substitute for a message that resonates with voters. Ramaswamy entered the race as a prominent Trump ally with considerable resources, but Acton kept the focus on household costs, healthcare and her Ohio roots.His defeat does not establish that Ohio has permanently shifted away from Republicans. It does, however, show how a high-profile candidate can lose ground when national political loyalties, controversial campaign tactics and local economic concerns collide.For Republicans, the result raises questions about how closely candidates should align themselves with Trump in elections where voters are also judging the administration's record. For Democrats, Acton's victory offers a potential model for competing in a state that has Republican domination in recent presidential elections.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s aggressive campaign push in the final weeks before the midterm elections failed to prevent a sweeping Republican defeat, with
articles.body: US President Donald Trump’s aggressive campaign push in the final weeks before the midterm elections failed to prevent a sweeping Republican defeat, with party insiders increasingly blaming the president for the growing public anger that fuelled the Democratic resurgence.Just weeks before voters headed to the polls, Republicans were already struggling to contain mounting losses across dozens of races. The party’s House majority was slipping away, while control of the Senate, once considered safely Republican, had turned into a competitive battle. Trump responded by embarking on an intensive campaign tour, travelling across the country to energise voters in traditionally Republican strongholds.But the effort came too late to reverse the political damage. According to CNN, the president repeatedly questioned how the party had reached such a difficult position, asking those around him: "How did we get here?"Republicans, however, believed the answer lay partly in his own decisions. An unidentified Texas-based GOP operative told CNN ahead of Election Day: "People are so mad. And Trump hasn’t done anything to help any of that."The anger stemmed from a combination of economic anxiety and dissatisfaction with the administration's policies. The unpopular war with Iran, rising fuel prices and persistent inflation had intensified concerns over the cost of living, pushing Trump's approval ratings to record lows.The economic discontent was reflected in the AP Voter Poll, which found that around three-quarters of voters considered the economy either 'not so good' or 'poor'. Nearly eight in 10 said inflation had caused moderate or severe financial hardship for their households. Government corruption and concerns that Trump prioritised his personal interests over the country's also emerged as major issues.Trump's campaign push fails to stop Democratic waveThe scale of the Republican defeat became increasingly apparent as Democrats made gains in states and congressional districts that had long been considered conservative territory.Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, with Republicans losing several House districts that Trump had carried by more than 10 percentage points in the previous presidential election. The victories included James Talarico's breakthrough Senate win in Texas and Annie Andrews' upset victory in South Carolina.Democrats also made significant gains in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and North Carolina, while Republican candidates backed by Trump struggled to hold their ground. His endorsement of scandal-hit Texas candidate Ken Paxton, in particular, had raised concerns among Republicans before the election.The results exposed cracks in the coalition that had helped Trump return to the White House, with younger voters and Latinos shifting away from Republicans, according to the AP Voter Poll.Despite spending much of the final month campaigning almost daily, Trump could not prevent the electoral backlash. Republicans had also poured millions of dollars into competitive races and traditionally safe districts, but their financial advantage failed to stop the Democratic surge.Trump distances himself from Republican lossesAs the results began emerging, Trump sought to separate himself from the defeat, arguing that he had not been on the ballot."I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" he wrote on his social media platform.In a late-night interview with Fox News, Trump also dismissed the idea that the results represented a personal defeat, saying voters "didn't like the candidates".However, the Democratic takeover of Congress threatens to significantly constrain the remainder of his presidency. Democratic leaders have indicated that investigations into senior administration officials, scrutiny of Trump's business interests and possible impeachment proceedings could feature prominently in their agenda.The election results have therefore dealt Trump more than a setback at the ballot box, leaving his administration facing an increasingly hostile Congress for the final two years of his term.You use AI every day. articles.title: King Charles sold a young racehorse to Australian owners just months before it won the Melbourne Cup on only its sixth career start; the horse led its new trainer to an unprecedented sweep of the top three
articles.summary: Racing rarely brings out stories this amusing.
articles.body: Racing rarely brings out stories this amusing. A young colt once owned by King Charles III was sold to Australian interests, placed in Ciaron Maher’s stable, and then produced the performance of his short career in the race Australia stops for. The horse named Point of Law won the Melbourne Cup at Flemington on November 3, 2026, in only his sixth career start, having never previously raced over the demanding 3,200 metre distance, according to AFP.The victory carried an extra twist. Maher did not merely train the winner. His horses finished first, second and third, with Point of Law leading home stablemates Zahrann and Juja Kibo. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported that this was the first time in the Melbourne Cup’s 166 editions that one trainer had filled the entire top three.For Maher, it was a second Melbourne Cup triumph, but the scale of this result was entirely different. For Ethan Brown, the jockey who rode Point of Law, it was a first success in Australia’s most famous race. And for the horse’s former royal owners, it was the kind of result that turns a routine sale into an unforgettable piece of racing folklore. Read more about this unexpected twist-of-fate story, as per ABC and AFP reports, here:A royal sale that became a headlinePoint of Law began his racing life in Britain, where he was previously owned by King Charles and Queen Camilla. He was then purchased by Maher, making Australia his new racing home and setting up the remarkable sequence that followed. AFP described the purchase as Maher’s acquisition from King Charles, with the Melbourne Cup representing the colt’s Australian debut. That detail gives the result its human appeal. Racing owners sell horses for many practical reasons, from stable planning to bloodstock strategy, and few could have predicted that this particular three-year-old would become the central figure in a Melbourne Cup for the ages. The sale did not simply change Point of Law’s address. It placed him with a trainer capable of preparing him for one of the toughest staying tests in world racing.By the time he reached Flemington, Point of Law had already signalled that something special might be coming. He won the Geelong Cup in his Australian debut, a lead-up performance that excited bookmakers and gave Maher confidence that the horse could handle the step up in distance. AFP noted that he entered the Melbourne Cup as a short-priced favourite after that powerful Geelong display.A race built for a stayerThe Melbourne Cup is not a sprint disguised as a marathon. Run over 3,200 metres, it tests stamina, patience, balance and nerve. It has been contested since 1861 and remains such a major part of Victorian life that race day is a public holiday in the state. This year’s renewal developed in unusually dramatic fashion. Royal Supremacy, another Maher runner, broke from barrier 21 and went forward early. By the 1,500 metre mark, he had opened an eight-length lead over the 23-horse field. With 1,000 metres remaining, that advantage had stretched to 20 lengths, creating the kind of front-running spectacle that can either become a famous steal or collapse into a cautionary tale.Royal Supremacy kept finding more for longer than most expected. He still held a commanding 12-length lead at the 400 metre mark, according to the ABC. But the final Flemington straight is long, and the pace eventually began to tell. Point of Law, ridden patiently by Brown, emerged from behind the leaders and swept past with about 150 metres to run.The winning margin was 3.75 lengths. It was not a narrow scramble, but a decisive change of momentum in the closing stages, with the favourite showing the acceleration that separates a good stayer from a genuine Cup winner.Maher’s unprecedented trifectaMaher had seven runners in the race, an extraordinary commitment in itself. Yet even he could not have scripted the outcome. Point of Law won, Zahrann finished second and Juja Kibo took third, giving the stable the first trainer-led trifecta in Melbourne Cup history.“This is what the Melbourne Cup is all about,” Maher said after the race, according to the ABC. He described Point of Law as a horse that had thrived and thanked his team and owners for their work throughout the campaign. He also called the achievement of having three horses fill the top three positions remarkable.The result was especially striking because Maher’s other runners did not simply disappear. Royal Supremacy, after his bold front-running effort, finished fifth. Shockletz was sixth. Only Mr Monaco failed to make an impact, coming home 17th. That depth of performance underlined that this was not a lucky result for one horse but an exceptionally strong training performance across an entire team.Brown’s moment to rememberFor Brown, the win carried a personal weight beyond the trophy. It was his first Melbourne Cup victory, and he rode the race with the calm assurance of someone who understood that the early leader might not be the horse to follow. His decision to wait, then deliver Point of Law at the right time, proved decisive.Afterwards, Brown struggled to put the experience into words. “Don’t wake me up. Amazing feeling,” he told AFP. He also praised Maher for standing by him through earlier mistakes and continuing to give him opportunities on important horses.The ABC reported that Brown reflected on Maher’s support since he was around 22 years old, saying the trainer had believed in him despite errors on his horses. When Brown collected the trophy, he admitted he had to pinch himself. It was a reminder that, for all the money, history and spectacle surrounding the Melbourne Cup, the sport still turns on individual relationships between trainers, jockeys and horses.A new chapter for Point of LawPoint of Law’s story now has an almost improbable shape. A three-year-old formerly owned by Britain’s King is sold to Australia, joins one of the country’s leading stables, wins a major lead-up race, then captures the Melbourne Cup at his sixth career start. AFP emphasised that he had never raced beyond 3,200 metres before Flemington, making the performance even more impressive.The horse’s next chapters will be watched closely. Winners of the Melbourne Cup instantly become part of Australian racing history, and Point of Law has already earned a place among the race’s most memorable champions. But whatever comes next, Tuesday’s result will be remembered for more than the trophy.It will be remembered as the day a former royal racehorse repaid his new connections in the most public way possible, while helping his trainer achieve something no one had managed in 166 runnings of the race. As Maher put it, it has been a whirlwind. For Australian racing, it was also a day that showed why the Melbourne Cup continues to capture imaginations far beyond the track.You use AI every day. articles.body: Trump asked America to pretend he was on the ballot. On Wednesday, voters delivered their verdict on his presidency anyway.A historic Democratic wave swept across the United States, handing the party control of both chambers of Congress and delivering a sweeping rebuke to President Donald Trump and his Republican allies. The results went well beyond the usual midterm setback for a ruling party as Democrats made breakthroughs in states and constituencies that had remained Republican strongholds for decades, signalling a dramatic shift in the political mood halfway through Trump's second presidency.The scale of the reversal was particularly striking in the Senate. Democrats captured seats in Kansas, Texas, South Carolina, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio while also making significant gains in the House of Representatives. The party's resurgence extended to statehouses, where Democrats won governorships and dismantled Republican legislative advantages. In Texas, a state that had not elected a Democratic governor since the 1990s, Gina Hinojosa's victory was emblematic of the scale of the shift.Follow US midterm results 2026 live updatesThe results also exposed the limits of Trump's personal influence. He had urged supporters to treat the midterms as a referendum on his presidency and invested heavily in candidates who embraced his MAGA agenda. But several of his high-profile endorsements failed to translate into victories. Republican losses in traditionally conservative territory, alongside reversals among Latino and rural voters, suggest that the electoral coalition that powered Trump's return to the White House is facing fresh challenges.Here are top 10 winners and losers of US midterm elections 2026:WINNERS1. DemocratsWith a sweeping return to power in Washington and a resurgence across Middle America, the Democratic Party has achieved what appeared difficult just months ago. Its victories in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa are particularly significant because these states had become increasingly difficult terrain for Democrats.The party also made inroads among Latino voters and in rural constituencies, reversing some of the gains Republicans had made during the Trump era. In the Rust Belt and Great Plains, Democrats have reclaimed ground in states such as Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota and Iowa.The victory gives Democrats control of congressional committees, investigative powers and the ability to obstruct Trump's legislative priorities. Just as importantly, the party now has a new generation of potential national leaders emerging from state-level victories. The challenge will be converting this anti-Trump wave into a sustainable political coalition ahead of 2028.2. Abdul El-SayedEl-Sayed's victory in Michigan is one of the most consequential individual outcomes of this election. The 42-year-old physician and former public health official defeated Republican Mike Rogers, making history as the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate. His victory marks a significant milestone for Muslim representation in American politics, particularly at a time when debates over immigration, identity and America's role in the Middle East have become increasingly polarised.His victory is also significant for the Democratic Party's ideological debate. El-Sayed ran on a progressive platform centred on universal healthcare, working-class economics and restrictions on American military support for Israel.He had faced resistance from sections of the Democratic establishment, while outside groups spent heavily against him. His campaign's success demonstrates that progressive candidates can compete in electorally important states despite opposition from powerful political and financial interests. It could also strengthen the progressive wing's voice in debates over US policy in the Middle East.3. Indian-AmericansThe Indian-American community consolidated its presence in US electoral politics, with victories across congressional and state-level contests.Democrat Pia Dandiya won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, while incumbent Suhas Subramanyam secured re-election in Virginia. Maryland Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller also won another term alongside Governor Wes Moore.4. IranIran has emerged as a most important beneficiary of the Democratic victory, particularly as Trump's handling of the conflict becomes a subject of greater congressional scrutiny.The administration's military actions against Iran have been politically contentious. With Democrats now controlling Congress, the White House faces a more difficult environment for securing legislative support, defending military expenditure and managing the domestic political consequences of an extended conflict.The change does not give Tehran a veto over American military action as Trump retains considerable authority as commander-in-chief, but the political calculations have changed. Congressional investigations, funding debates and demands for greater accountability could raise the domestic cost of escalation with Iran.5. IndiaFor New Delhi, the Democratic win could open up a fresh opportunity to recalibrate its trade negotiations with Washington. A politically weakened Trump may be keen to secure a quick trade deal with India to demonstrate economic and diplomatic success, particularly after facing setbacks involving Russia, China and Iran, according to Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).While the Democratic victory is unlikely to change the broader protectionist trade approach of the US, it could allow India to push for a more balanced agreement.LOSERS6. Donald TrumpThe midterm results handed out the biggest political setback to Trump and his second presidency. By losing both chambers, Republicans have surrendered the legislative advantage that allowed the president to pursue his agenda with relatively little resistance.Trump had personally invested himself in the election, urging Republicans to vote as though he were on the ballot. But his endorsements failed to save several prominent candidates, while Democrats made breakthroughs in traditionally Republican territory.The consequences could be substantial. Democratic-controlled committees can investigate the administration, scrutinise government contracts and spending, summon officials and demand documents. Trump's legislative priorities, including further tax and spending measures, will face a hostile Congress.He still retains executive powers, particularly in foreign policy and trade, but governing will become considerably more difficult. The results also raise a bigger question for Republicans: can Trump's political formula continue to deliver victories beyond his own presidential campaigns?7. Elon MuskTesla and SpaceX chief's massive political investment failed to deliver the Republican congressional victory he was seeking. The world's richest man spent around $366 million on the 2026 midterm election by October, making him one of the biggest political donors in the country.His America PAC backed Republican candidates in several competitive races, including Texas, Ohio and Michigan. The Texas Senate contest was particularly important as Musk's political operation supported Republican Ken Paxton against Democrat James Talarico.Paxton lost, while Democrats also made significant gains in other races where Musk-backed candidates were competing.The implications, however, may be far beyond the capital loss. Musk has benefited from his proximity to the Trump administration, particularly through his involvement in government efficiency initiatives and his business interests. A Democratic-controlled House could increase scrutiny of federal contracts, regulatory decisions and his previous government role.8. Vivek RamaswamyRamaswamy's defeat in Ohio is a setback for a politician who had emerged as one of the most prominent younger faces of the Trump-aligned Republican movement.Despite Trump's backing and his national profile, Ramaswamy could not convert his political visibility into a gubernatorial victory. Democrat Amy Acton defeated him, becoming the first woman elected governor of Ohio.Ramaswamy had positioned himself as a representative of a new generation of Republican leadership. His campaign also drew on themes that had become central to the MAGA movement, including opposition to progressive politics and an aggressive approach to government reform.His defeat therefore raises questions about whether the political appeal of the Trump movement can be successfully transferred to younger candidates.It also complicates Ramaswamy's own political ambitions and his national profile.9. JD VanceThe midterm results pose a direct challenge for JD Vance, who has been widely discussed as a potential successor to Trump in 2028.As vice-president, Vance was among the administration's most prominent campaigners, defending Trump's agenda and rallying Republican voters. But the results have exposed the vulnerabilities of the political coalition he may eventually seek to inherit.The losses in Ohio are especially relevant. Ramaswamy's gubernatorial defeat and Republican Jon Husted's Senate loss represent a setback in Vance's home state.The larger problem is the Republican succession battle. Vance's appeal has been closely associated with Trump's political movement, but the midterms raise questions about his influence.The vice president now faces a complicated political task - retain the loyalty of Trump's core supporters while developing an identity that can attract a wider electorate. The 2028 Republican race remains open, but the midterms have made the path to becoming the undisputed heir to MAGA less straightforward.10. Israel lobbyThe election has exposed growing resistance to the traditional pro-Israel consensus in American politics, particularly within the Democratic Party.The most prominent example is Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, whose opposition to unconditional American military support for Israel became a defining feature of his campaign. His victory came despite substantial spending by pro-Israel political groups against him.According to campaign finance data compiled by VoteLog, the United Democracy Project, AIPAC's affiliated super PAC, spent more than $30 million in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, including over $20 million opposing El-Sayed.His subsequent victory in the general election gives progressive Democrats a prominent example to cite in their argument that criticism of Israeli government policy and American military assistance need not be an electoral liability.The implications for AIPAC and other pro-Israel lobbying organisations could be significant. They will continue to have financial resources and access to lawmakers, but the political environment within the Democratic Party is changing. The question is whether their traditional influence over candidate selection and foreign-policy debates can withstand a more vocal progressive challenge.Bonus losers: Asim Munir and Shehbaz SharifPakistan's renewed engagement with Washington under Trump could face a more complicated political environment after the Democratic takeover of Congress.Islamabad has invested heavily in rebuilding its relationship with the Trump administration, with PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir cultivating closer ties with the US president. Pakistan has also sought to position itself as an important interlocutor in the Iran conflict, while pursuing cooperation on trade, minerals and security.Much of this diplomatic momentum has been associated with Trump's personal engagement and the administration's regional priorities. A Democratic-controlled Congress could now subject aspects of that relationship to greater scrutiny.After the loss of Trump's party, Islamabad may find that personal access to the president is no longer sufficient.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘You could smell alcohol on his breath’: Rahul Gandhi targets Bhagwant Mann over drug menace
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday slammed Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann, accusing him of failing to tackle the state's drug
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday slammed Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann, accusing him of failing to tackle the state's drug problem and alleging that he used to smell of alcohol during their time together in Parliament.Addressing the party's 'Insaaf Rally' in Sangrur, Rahul also accused the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) government of being controlled by leaders in Delhi and questioned its ability to curb drug abuse.Recalling his time in the Lok Sabha with the Punjab CM, Rahul said, “I was in the Lok Sabha with him. He (Punjab CM) used to sit with us and tell jokes, right there, sitting among us. By 11:00 am, you could smell alcohol on his breath.”He clarified that drinking was a personal choice but said the chief minister's conduct was relevant to the state's fight against substance abuse.“Now, I am not saying that Bhagwant Mann shouldn’t drink; that is his personal affair. If he chooses to drink, that is entirely his own business. But if you truly want to fight the menace of substance abuse, your Chief Minister cannot be under the influence every single evening. You need someone who will fight for Punjab, someone who genuinely feels the pain caused by drugs, someone who carries the pain of Punjab in his heart,” he said.Rahul further alleged that the Punjab government was being run from Delhi with AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal and Union home minister Amit Shah exercising influence over the state government.“People here need a govt that works for Punjab. When the Congress party comes to power, the govt of Punjab cannot be run from Delhi. Our party will run the Punjab government from within Punjab” he said.“Right now, however, the reins are held half by Amit Shah and half by Kejriwal, while Bhagwant Mann just sits there. Punjab is being governed from Delhi,” he added.Rahul also questioned Amit Shah's claim that the drug menace in Punjab would be eradicated within three years.“What timeline did they (Union HM Amit Shah) set for the drug issue?... Within three years? In three years, Amit Shah won’t even be the Home Minister anymore... My assessment is that this govt won’t even last a year. Anyway, Amit Shah claims he will eradicate the drug problem in three years,” he said.Recalling his earlier warnings about the spread of drugs in Punjab, Rahul said opposition parties including the BJP and the Shiromani Akali Dal had dismissed his concerns at the time.“Many years ago, when I first visited Punjab, I pointed out that the drug menace was spreading there. The opposition, the BJP, the Akali Dal, and others, claimed that Rahul Gandhi knew nothing about Punjab and that drugs were not spreading in the state,” he said.He argued that Punjab needed industries, factories and a strong agricultural sector to create opportunities for people, warning that a lack of economic opportunities could contribute to drug abuse and gangsterism.The Congress leader accused the AAP government of failing to deliver on its promise to eliminate drugs from the state.“The Aam Aadmi Party came to power, and you placed your trust in them, in Bhagwant Mann and the Aam Aadmi Party. They promised that they would eradicate the drug menace. I ask you: where have they eliminated it? From which corner of Punjab have they managed to remove drugs? They are simply incapable of eradicating this menace,” Rahul said.The Congress leader also referred to his challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a face-to-face debate, which he said he had issued a day earlier.“Yesterday, I challenged Narendra Modi to a face-to-face debate. He can make anyone he wants the judge for this debate. I guarantee the nation that Narendra Modi cannot sit before me," Rahul said."I can guarantee that within five minutes of the debate starting I will prove that Narendra Modi is a 'desh-drohi' and Donald Trump controls him,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Florida woman sentenced to three years in prison for pretending to be the family of a teenager killed in the Texas floods to create fake GoFundMe and SpotFund pages
articles.summary: Fake GoFundMe and SpotFund pages created after the 2025 Texas floods have ended in a three-year prison sentence for Maitlin White, a 29-year-old from
articles.body: Fake GoFundMe and SpotFund pages created after the 2025 Texas floods have ended in a three-year prison sentence for Maitlin White, a 29-year-old from Crestview, Florida, who pleaded guilty to two counts of online impersonation in Harris County, Texas. White pretended to be the father of Chloe Childress, a 19-year-old from Houston who died in Kerr County while working as a counsellor at Camp Mystic. The pages used the father’s name, Chloe’s photograph and an account of the family’s loss to appeal for donations, according to court records. Both appeared less than a week after the floods struck Central Texas.How a father’s alert led detectives to two fake fundraising pages in his daughter’s nameFOX 26 Houston reported that Childress’s father alerted authorities to the fake GoFundMe campaign. A detective then learned of a second campaign on SpotFund that also used the names of Chloe and her father. Records requested from both platforms listed White as the creator of each page, according to the court documents. The SpotFund campaign was linked to her Chime checking account. Records did not show how much money either campaign raised.What the woman told a detective after admitting she made both pages for quick moneyAccording to FOX 26 Houston, the documents say the detective found White’s phone number and recorded a call with her. She admitted making the campaigns using Chloe’s likeness and her father’s name, and described herself as a single mother with young children looking for a quick way to earn. Court records also state that she is a single mother of two and that she set up the fake page using her mobile phone.Plea deal accepted on a Friday morning, with 111 days of credit for time served and a GoFundMe banCourt records show White accepted the plea deal on a Friday morning and will receive 111 days of credit for time already served. GoFundMe has banned her account from future fundraising on the platform.Harris County Constable Precinct One Alan Rosen, who confirmed the sentence, said in a statement published by KPRC that White preyed on the emotions of the community and abused a family already enduring an unimaginable tragedy. He called her conduct inexcusable and said the case should serve as a warning to anyone planning similar schemes. He added that a family devastated by the loss of their daughter did not need someone profiting from her name.How to check a donation page is genuine before giving money to flood victims’ familiesRosen urged people who want to help flood victims to do some homework and vet the source before giving, even though the urge to donate quickly is strong. The Texas Attorney General’s Office issued an alert on the same Friday telling Texans to avoid wire transfers and to avoid confirming personal or financial information, so that support reaches legitimate organisations. The warnings come as floodwaters are rising again in the same region one year on, KPRC reported.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: The picture that defines  MAGA's midterms loss: A Republican mocked Indian kids watching football. Then Texas turned blue
articles.summary: A viral photograph of Indian students celebrating a football victory becomes the symbol of the Republican Party's unexpected midterm loss in Texas. Explore the political ramifications and racial tensions exposed by Bo French's controversial comments.
articles.body: A picture, they say, is worth a thousand words. A bright starry night immediately makes one think of a talented artist who cut off his own ear. A man reaching out to God immediately makes one think of the Sistine Chapel and, with it, the role Christianity has played in being the edifice of modern Western civilisation. And now a bunch of Indian students celebrating a college football win will forever be etched as the definitive picture of MAGA’s midterm loss.But let’s start from scratch. Many years ago, a Conservative politician in the UK named Norman Tebbit came up with the Tebbit Test to test an immigrant’s loyalty: If an immigrant’s home country played England in a cricket match, did the immigrant back England or his home country?Recently, a Texan politician named Bo French, no wonder Butch Coolidge said in Pulp Fiction: “I'm an American, honey. Our names don't mean s***”, gave the most asinine reinterpretation of the Tebbit Test, which shall henceforth be known as the French Test.Posting a picture of Texas students celebrating a famous football win, French wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”The photograph came from the University of Texas Longhorns' extraordinary 24-23 comeback victory over Ohio State on September 12. The students were wearing burnt orange, making the famous Hook 'em Horns gesture and celebrating an American football victory. Yet French, the Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, saw something considerably more sinister: evidence that Americans were being displaced by foreigners. Among those photographed was Dhairya Gupta, a naturalised American citizenThe photograph quickly travelled through the MAGA ecosystem, attracting the usual comments about Bollywood, cricket and the demographic transformation of America. Nick Fuentes, the far-right commentator and leader of the Groyper movement, declared it “the most evocative image in recent memory of white replacement”. He devoted part of his programme to what he called the "Indian takeover of Texas".French's remarks even managed to provoke an increasingly rare phenomenon in American politics: bipartisan outrage. Republican Senator John Cornyn condemned the comments, while former George W Bush strategist Karl Rove announced his support for French's Democratic opponent, Jon Rosenthal. Several Republican lawmakers demanded an apology. French refused, dismissing his critics as insufficiently conservative.And then the controversy became financially consequential.According to the Texas Tribune, Rosenthal, previously an obscure Democratic candidate, raised approximately $488,000 during the July-September reporting period, much of it following French's viral remarks. Contributions arrived from every American state except North Dakota. French subsequently raised $748,000 in the next reporting period, indicating that the controversy energised donors on both sides.Incidentally, the Texas Railroad Commission regulates oil and gas, not railways, which is almost as misleading as French's understanding of American citizenship. Perhaps he should have spent more time studying oil wells and less time studying the complexions of college students.Then came November 3.French lost to Rosenthal, who became the first Democrat elected to the commission in decades. But the larger shock was unfolding across Texas. Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott to become the state's first Democratic governor since Ann Richards. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton to win a US Senate seat. Democrats captured several other statewide offices, ending a Republican electoral dominance that had appeared unassailable since 1994.It would be tempting to construct a neat political morality tale in which Republicans insulted Indians and consequently lost Texas. Reality, particularly electoral reality, is rarely so accommodating. The results establish no such cause-and-effect relationship. But the photograph offers a remarkable window into the identity politics, demographic anxieties and political contradictions that had been building across the Lone Star State.To understand those contradictions, one needs to travel north from Austin to Frisco, a prosperous Dallas suburb where nearly one in five residents is Indian.For years, Indian immigrants helped transform Frisco into a thriving centre of technology, medicine and business. But in 2026, its City Council meetings also became a forum for complaints about an alleged Indian takeover. Speakers attacked H-1B visas, demographic change and the growing Indian population. At one demonstration, an Indian flag was torn apart while protesters shouted abuse against India.Among those listening was Burt Thakur, an Indian-born US Navy veteran, Trump supporter and Republican councillor. Thakur had served in the American military, acquired citizenship, embraced conservative politics and won an American election. Yet he found himself confronting people questioning whether Indians belonged in his city.Even a video of Indian-American Boy Scouts reciting the Pledge of Allegiance attracted racist abuse. Thakur wondered how children performing one of America's most recognisable patriotic rituals could simultaneously be accused of failing to assimilate.The hostility extended beyond immigration. In Sugar Land, conservative activist Jesse Hughes threatened to tear down a 90-foot Hanuman statue on private temple property if his political side prevailed. The Coalition of Hindus of North America (CoHNA) condemned the threat as religious bigotry.Nor were disputes involving Hindu identity confined to MAGA or America. In France, BAPS became embroiled in controversy over the exclusion of female Eiffel Tower employees during a religious delegation's visit. A subsequent investigation found that women had indeed been moved, but that the organisation had not explicitly requested their exclusion. The incidents were different, but each fed wider arguments over the place of Hindu religious practices in Western public life.And these incidents unfolded against a measurable increase in online hostility.A September report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH) found that the monthly volume of anti-South Asian hate posts on X had increased 240% between January 2024 and June 2026. Researchers identified more than half a million such posts between January 2025 and June 2026 alone. Nearly 45% involved narratives portraying South Asians as invaders, job thieves or demographic threats, often invoking H-1B visas and immigration.The findings covered South Asians broadly, rather than Indians exclusively, and measured online discourse rather than the prevalence of racist attitudes among American voters. Nevertheless, they provide important context for how a photograph of students celebrating a sporting victory could become material for an argument about racial replacement.There is something particularly curious about this hostility because Indian-Americans have, by conventional measures, done remarkably well in America.According to the Pew Research Center, the median annual income of Indian-headed households stood at $151,200 in 2023, compared with $105,600 for Asian-headed households overall. The Migration Policy Institute found that 82% of Indian immigrant adults aged 25 and above held at least a bachelor's degree in 2024. Indian-origin executives lead companies such as Microsoft and Google, while the community has become increasingly visible in medicine, academia, entrepreneurship and American politics.There are more than five million people of Indian origin in the country. Yet economic success and elite representation have not necessarily translated into a collective political voice or immunity from prejudice.For years, Indian-Americans were celebrated as a model minority, people whose educational and professional accomplishments appeared to validate the American Dream. But that success has increasingly become a source of resentment in some online circles, where Indian professionals are accused of nepotism, visa fraud or stealing American jobs, often without evidence.Of course, legitimate questions exist about the H-1B programme, labour-market competition and corporate immigration practices. But questioning immigration policy is different from deciding that American citizens are foreigners because of their appearance.The political contradiction becomes even more striking when one remembers what Republicans were doing just two years earlier.In 2024, the Collin County Republican Party had put up Trump-Vance campaign signs in Hindi, Telugu, Gujarati and Tamil to woo Indian-American voters. Sreekanth Reddy, who helped organise the outreach, subsequently found himself confronting anti-Indian rhetoric within the political movement he supported.And the outreach had not been entirely unsuccessful.Donald Trump had made notable gains among Indian-Americans in 2024, particularly younger men, as part of his broader effort to expand the Republican coalition.According to the Carnegie Endowment's Indian American Attitudes Survey, Trump's support rose from 22% in 2020 to 30% in 2024. Among Indian-American men aged 18 to 39, it reached 40%.The appeal was hardly inexplicable. Many Indian-Americans are entrepreneurs, professionals and business owners who favour lower taxation, economic opportunity and, in some cases, socially conservative policies. Others had grown increasingly uncomfortable with Democratic identity politics.But two years into Trump's second presidency, there were signs that these Republican gains had evaporated.The Carnegie Endowment's October 2026 survey, released just before the midterms, found that 62% of Indian-American citizens intended to vote Democratic in congressional elections, compared with only 19% supporting Republicans. Among younger Indian-American men, Republican congressional voting intentions stood at 23%, compared with the 40% who had supported Trump in 2024.An important qualification: the surveys compared presidential preferences with congressional voting intentions, not the behaviour of the same individuals. In fact, Carnegie found that much of the Republican decline among younger Indian-American men was already visible in January 2026, months before French posted the photograph. The controversy cannot explain a political shift that had substantially preceded it.Another Carnegie finding was particularly revealing. Among Indian-Americans intending to vote Democratic, 35% said their primary motivation was opposition to Republicans rather than support for Democrats.Indian-Americans might not particularly love Democrats, whose identity politics and treatment of Hindu concerns can also alienate sections of the community. But that dissatisfaction does not automatically make them Republicans.And there is another complication. A 2026 survey by Asian Texans for Justice found that 40% of Asian Texans identified as Republicans, compared with 31% as Democrats. That survey covered Asian Texans broadly, not just Indian-Americans. It suggests that the state's political alignments cannot simply be inferred from national Indian-American polling.Nor can we establish that Indian-Americans swung the Texas election. While community organisers reported increased early voting in neighbourhoods with substantial Indian populations in Collin County, higher turnout does not establish which candidates those voters supported.The statewide Democratic victory had much larger explanations. Hinojosa campaigned on affordability, public education and dissatisfaction with Republican leadership. Talarico benefited from broader discontent over prices, the Iran war and national politics. The Republican defeat involved Hispanic voters, younger Americans and other constituencies far beyond the Indian-American community.None of this diminishes the photograph's significance. It simply means the photograph is better understood as a symbol of an extraordinary political moment than as proof of what caused it.For Republicans, the contradiction was stark. A party that had worked to win over Indian-Americans was simultaneously confronting a strain of political activism that questioned whether those same people belonged in America. Several Republicans condemned French, while others defended him. Some Indian-American Republicans continued to challenge the hostility without abandoning their party.The image itself even provoked an uncomfortable debate within the University of Texas. Emails obtained by the Texas Tribune revealed that students and alumni had urged university leaders to condemn French more explicitly. One Indian-American student, who had lived in California their entire life, wanted the university president to look into a camera and tell them they belonged in Texas.That may be the most revealing detail of the entire controversy. For all the talk of immigration, foreign workers and demographic replacement, the students in the photograph were not trying to make a political statement. They were celebrating a football victory at their university.Then, less than two months later, the politician who made them a national controversy lost his election, along with a succession of Republican candidates across Texas.One election cannot establish whether a state has permanently changed its political character. Nor can a single photograph explain an electoral reversal involving millions of voters.But photographs do not always become historical symbols because they explain everything. Sometimes they endure because they capture a contradiction more clearly than a thousand arguments ever could.Bo French looked at the photograph and believed he could see what was wrong with Texas.The election did not prove him responsible for what happened next.It did, however, produce an answer he probably wasn't expecting.You use AI every day. articles.title: Donald the 'lame' duck: Trump loses House & Senate, but can he be stopped?
articles.summary: Donald, it's done bro.
articles.body: Donald, it's done bro.The phrase (coined by Salman Khan) has basically become a major part of Indian politics with parties across lines using it to one up each other in the ever lasting loop of the electoral cycle.But for the 45th & 47th POTUS, the phrase may signal things to come.Trump who won 312 votes from the electoral college and secured 49.8% of the popular vote, may now be described as a "lame duck" president.Wednesday's results confirm what the pollsters have been predicting in the midterms. A majority for the Dems in both the House and the Senate.With both chambers now painted blue, Trump's agenda which was already facing scruitny is now all but stuck in the political quagmire.And, by the time the next cycle comes around Trump will no longer be the POTUS nor can he (legally) contest again.The real estate baron-turned-politician may have suffered a major setback, but declaring the end of his grip on American politics would be premature. The midterm results will undoubtedly limit Trump's agenda, but counting out the MAGA founder has rarely been a safe bet.Having defied expectations in 2024, Trump has repeatedly shown a knack for pulling a card out of his sleeve when the odds appear stacked against him.So, is it too early to write the political obituary of Trump or would it be premature to draw the curtain on the MAGA founder? Let's break it down.History of the 'lame duck'Within hours of the polls closing, White House communications director Steven Cheung posted a reminder: “Still your President!” The message was mocked online, with users describing Donald Trump as a lame duck.The phrase dates to 18th-century London, where it described a stockbroker unable to meet his debts. In American politics, it describes an office-holder whose influence is fading. Trump, however, has more than two years left in office. A weakened president is not necessarily powerless.Democrats have won control of both chambers. The Senate is projected to have 54 Democrats and independents who caucus with them, against 44 Republicans, with two races uncalled. They flipped at least seven Republican-held seats and more than two dozen House districts. The last president to lose both chambers in a midterm election was George W Bush in 2006.Republicans remain in control until the new Congress is sworn in on January 3, 2027. After that, Democrats can block legislation, reject nominees and investigate the administration, but they cannot control the executive branch.A blue wave, state by stateIn Texas, Democrat James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton with about 55% of the vote, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988. In Maine, Troy Jackson defeated incumbent Susan Collins. Democrats also flipped seats in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina.Democrats also flipped more than two dozen House districts and won Republican-held governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas. Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House, subject to a vote in January. High living costs, the Iran war and corruption concerns all featured in voters' frustrations. Trump congratulated Democrats but blamed some Republican candidates for the losses.Russia And Ukraine: Congress can help, but cannot make peaceFor Kyiv, a Democratic Congress may offer a more sympathetic audience, but it will not automatically change the White House's approach. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, backs legislation for security, economic and intelligence support to Ukraine. Democrats can use hearings and funding to keep assistance on the agenda.Congress approved $400 million in military assistance, but the Pentagon has told lawmakers it will not complete the spending until fiscal year 2029, frustrating Democrats and some Republicans. Lawmakers can authorise money, but cannot dictate foreign policy.The administration's dealings with Moscow show the limits. On October 9, the US Treasury authorised transactions involving Russian-origin diesel. A week later, Trump waived sanctions provisions under the new Graham Act, arguing they could impede negotiations with Russia. Meeks criticised the move, saying it weakened pressure on Vladimir Putin.Democrats can challenge such decisions and make sanctions relief harder, but they cannot take charge of negotiations or replace presidential diplomacy.Iran: The war voters could not ignoreThe war with Iran has become one of the most politically costly parts of Trump's second term. It began on February 28, and Iran's response disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up energy costs. By late September, US petrol prices had reached around $4.50 a gallon.Democrats tried repeatedly to use war-powers votes to constrain the president. In June, a resolution advanced after four Republicans joined Democrats, but the Senate later blocked a further attempt, exposing divisions within the Republican ranks.Trump has not ruled out renewed military action, while indirect negotiations continue. Reuters reported on November 3 that Washington and Tehran remained far apart, with Iran demanding sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade before reopening the Strait. Trump said he was not seeking further conflict but would act if necessary.The president has significant authority to order military operations as commander-in-chief and does not always need prior congressional approval. But the 1973 War Powers Resolution requires him to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing US forces into hostilities. It also requires forces to be withdrawn within 60 days unless Congress authorises the operation, with a possible 30-day extension to complete withdrawal.Democrats can hold hearings, demand information and use funding legislation to apply pressure. Presidents of both parties have disputed the reach of the War Powers Resolution. After Democrats won Congress in 2006, George W Bush vetoed a bill tying Iraq war funding to a withdrawal timetable. Congress failed to override him and later approved funding without the deadline. The purse gives lawmakers leverage, but using it requires unity.Tariffs: A wall that keeps being rebuiltTrade policy is another front. On February 20, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the emergency powers law Trump had used to impose sweeping tariffs did not authorise them. He responded with a 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. That measure expired on July 24, after the law's 150-day limit.The administration has since relied on other laws, including Section 301 of the Trade Act and Section 232, which allows tariffs on national security grounds. It has also used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose duties on selected Canadian goods.Democrats want to restore Congress's control over trade policy. Chuck Schumer's End Trump's Tariff Tax Act, introduced with 28 co-sponsors, seeks to terminate and refund certain duties. Jeffries has made reversing the tariffs a priority. But any bill will need Trump's signature or a veto-proof majority. The Supreme Court has blocked one route, not the administration's use of other trade laws.Investigations: No easy removal, but plenty of problemsImpeachment may return to the conversation, but removing Trump is a much higher bar. The House can impeach by a simple majority. Conviction in the Senate requires a two-thirds vote of senators present, or 67 if all 100 attend. Democrats are well short of that threshold.Trump has already been impeached twice and acquitted twice by the Senate. Andrew Johnson and Bill Clinton were also acquitted after impeachment trials. Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 before the full House could vote. These precedents help explain why Democrats may focus first on investigations rather than make impeachment the centrepiece of their agenda.From January, Democratic-led House committees will gain the subpoena powers and resources that come with chairing the chamber. They are expected to examine the Jeffrey Epstein files, immigration enforcement, the Justice Department, presidential pardons and alleged conflicts of interest involving Trump's family and allies. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the Oversight Committee, wants to subpoena Attorney General Todd Blanche over the handling of the Epstein files. He has also signalled scrutiny of Trump family business dealings and donors to the proposed White House ballroom.The inquiries could force officials to answer questions in public, but subpoenas can be challenged in court. House Democrats' effort to secure testimony from former White House counsel Don McGahn, launched in 2019, took until 2021 to resolve. Investigations do not automatically bring down a president. Their impact depends on what they uncover.Healthcare, spending and judges: The other pressure pointsJeffries has promised to focus on affordability, including restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies and reversing nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts. Democrats can pass bills in the House, but major changes will need Senate support and Trump's signature. A Democratic House can, however, block spending bills and other Republican priorities.The 35-day shutdown of 2018-19 ended without Trump securing border-wall funding, but shutdowns disrupt public services and hurt federal workers. Democrats can also slow or block Cabinet and judicial appointments. Any Supreme Court vacancy would become a major political battle.Not over yet: The veto and the penAs results came in, he posted a picture of a red cap bearing one word: “Veto”. In a late-night Fox News interview, he said Democrats would eventually have to negotiate after he blocked their legislation.Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds of both chambers, usually 290 votes in the House and 67 in the Senate if all members vote. Democrats are nowhere near those numbers and would need substantial Republican support.Trump can also continue issuing executive orders and directing federal agencies, although courts can challenge them and a future president can reverse them. On returning to office in January 2025, Trump cancelled dozens of Joe Biden's orders. A Democrat could do the same in 2028.He can shape US diplomacy on Iran and Ukraine, decide how to approach Russia and China, and exercise the presidential pardon power. Congress can scrutinise those decisions, restrict funding and impose political costs, but it cannot take over diplomacy.So, can he be stopped?Partly. Democrats can investigate, delay and block legislation, making it harder for Trump to translate his agenda into law. But they cannot govern from Congress alone, and the veto remains a formidable shield.The next two years will depend on the courts, Republicans willing to break ranks and voters in 2028. Trump has lost Congress, not the presidency. The Trump era has entered a new phase, but the next two years are unlikely to be a quiet exit. Washington is about to learn how far a wounded duck can swim.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Jordan Adlard-Rogers inherited a £50m Cornwall estate after a DNA test; a UK jury has now found him guilty of grievous bodily harm in a 2024 pub fight
articles.summary: Jordan Adlard-Rogers became one of Britain’s most talked-about inheritance stories after a DNA test proved he was the son of aristocrat Charles Rogers,
articles.body: Jordan Adlard-Rogers became one of Britain’s most talked-about inheritance stories after a DNA test proved he was the son of aristocrat Charles Rogers, opening the way for him to inherit the £50 million Penrose Estate in Cornwall. Seven years later, the 38-year-old former community support worker has been convicted of grievous bodily harm after punching a man at a wedding reception in a Cornish pub, reported The Sun and Mirror UK.A jury at Truro Crown Court found Adlard-Rogers guilty after watching CCTV footage of the incident, which took place at the Out of the Blue pub in Porthleven on July 13, 2024. Prosecutors said the punch caused Sebastian Winzar to fall and suffer two fractures to his left leg, while Adlard-Rogers maintained that he acted in self-defence after being threatened and headbutted, as per Daily Mail and Mirror UK.The verdict brings a sharply different chapter to a life story that once seemed like a fairytale. Adlard-Rogers spent years trying to establish that Charles Rogers was his biological father, only for the DNA test to be carried out after the aristocrat’s death. He then inherited the 1,536-acre estate and spoke about using his new wealth to help local communities. Read more about him here, as per the reports:The night at the pubThe court heard that Adlard-Rogers and Winzar were acquaintances and had both been drinking at the pub during a wedding celebration. Winzar told jurors that Adlard-Rogers became aggressive, shouted at him and repeatedly asked him to go outside. He said he walked away several times but felt the defendant was trying to provoke a reaction.Winzar said the next thing he remembered was waking up in a chair with a broken leg. He suffered fractures in two places, a swollen lip and swelling to the back of his head. He spent five days in hospital and later underwent surgery on his left shin.CCTV footage shown to the jury became central to the case. Prosecutor Zoe Kuyken said, as per Daily Mail, it showed a disagreement between the two men, with Winzar bringing his face towards Adlard-Rogers before stepping back. She said Adlard-Rogers then swung his fist with force, causing Winzar to fall to the floor.Self-defence claim rejectedAdlard-Rogers admitted throwing a punch but told the court he did so to protect himself. He said Winzar had threatened him, told him he knew where he lived and came towards him in a way that made him fear another attack. “I punched him once, though not with much force,” he said in a prepared statement to police. His defence barrister, Robin Smith, argued that Winzar had been the aggressor and had headbutted Adlard-Rogers shortly before the punch. Smith said the footage showed his client trying to de-escalate matters and suggested that Winzar had repeatedly approached him in a threatening manner, as per the reports.The jury did not accept that account. After deliberating for just under two hours, jurors returned a unanimous guilty verdict for grievous bodily harm. Adlard-Rogers was asked in court whether he regretted his actions and replied that, at that particular time, he believed he had done “the right thing at the right time.”From care worker to estate heirThe conviction marks a striking reversal for a man whose life changed dramatically in 2019. Adlard-Rogers had long believed Charles Rogers could be his father, but the aristocrat repeatedly declined to take a DNA test while he was alive. Charles died in August 2019, and a test carried out after his death confirmed the family connection.With Charles’s mother and brother also deceased, Adlard-Rogers became the sole beneficiary of the Penrose Estate, a 1,536-acre property between Helston and Porthleven. The estate generates income through investments and by leasing land to local farmers.The Rogers family had given the estate to the National Trust in 1974 in exchange for a 1,000-year lease allowing family members to continue living there. After inheriting, Adlard-Rogers left his job and moved into the family’s historic home. He told reporters at the time that he wanted to set up a charity and support people in Porthleven and Helston.A complicated family historyThe inheritance story was never simple. Adlard-Rogers said he had known since the age of eight that Charles Rogers might be his father, but that early attempts to obtain a DNA test did not happen. He said he wrote letters in his twenties but received no reply, and later sent a final letter with a DNA test kit enclosed shortly before learning that Charles had died.Charles’s own life had been troubled. An inquest heard that he struggled with drug addiction and died from an overdose at the age of 62. Adlard-Rogers later reflected that his father had faced pressure to meet family expectations, including those created by his father’s naval career and his brother’s service as an RAF pilot.Despite the extraordinary change in circumstances, Adlard-Rogers said in 2019 that he did not want to forget where he had come from. He described worrying about the next bill earlier in life and said he hoped to use his position to help others.What happens nextJudge Simon Carr told Adlard-Rogers that all sentencing options remained available, including immediate custody. He warned the defendant to prepare himself for that possibility when he returns to court on December 11 for sentencing.The case will now be assessed alongside a probation report before the judge decides the appropriate punishment. For Adlard-Rogers, the outcome is a stark contrast to the public attention he received after inheriting the estate. The DNA test changed his legal status and financial future, but the jury’s verdict has now placed a serious criminal conviction at the centre of his story.You use AI every day.
