articles.title: SC rejects woman's plea to terminate six-month pregnancy over marital discord
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow a woman's plea for medical termination of her pregnancy which was over six months along citing
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday refused to allow a woman's plea for medical termination of her pregnancy which was over six months along citing marital discord with her husband.The case came before a bench of Justices B V Nagarathna and R Mahadevan, which had expressed concern over the request during an earlier hearing on Monday.The woman's husband opposed the termination, arguing that he too had a right over the unborn child and was willing to take care of the baby after birth.The bench said the case was different from those involving rape, sexual assault or foetal abnormalities, where termination may be permitted under the law.It questioned whether marital discord or alleged mistreatment by a husband and in-laws could, by itself, be grounds for ending an advanced pregnancy.“It is normal that wife talks against husband and husband talks against wife but it does not mean that you have to terminate the pregnancy on that ground. It is not a case of sexual assault or single woman becoming pregnant. Where are we heading as a society if the wife says that she wants termination of pregnancy because of her fight with the husband and in-laws... What about the right of the father,” the bench had said on Monday.The woman, who appeared before the bench virtually, said she did not want to continue the pregnancy and wanted a divorce. Her husband, however, urged the court not to allow the termination. He told the bench that he would take custody of the child after birth and look after it.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: From Iran to India: How Trump's midterm loss could affect America's foreign policy
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has faced the blues this midterm election, with Democrats sweeping both the House and Senate.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has faced the blues this midterm election, with Democrats sweeping both the House and Senate. As the president sees red over his party’s defeat, governments around the world are watching warily, weighing how the shift in congressional power could reshape Washington’s foreign policy and its approach to conflicts and alliances across the globe.Iran: Khamenei says US midterm results will not change Washington’s hostilityIran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said changes in the US political landscape would not alter Washington's hostility towards Tehran, after Republicans suffered setbacks in the midterm elections.“If anyone still hopes for a change in behaviour or a shift between political parties and factions in the system of domination, they are gravely mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written message published on his official website on Wednesday to mark Iran's annual November 4 anti-US commemoration.The message warned against making concessions to Washington, arguing that the US sought Iran's “unconditional surrender” and that any compromise would invite further demands and military attacks. It also portrayed Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz and against US military bases in the region as evidence that American military power was not invincible.“Any repetition of aggression will take on far broader dimensions,” the message said.Khamenei has not appeared in public or been heard speaking since the war began on February 28. No video or audio accompanied Wednesday's statement.Also read:How Trump's Iran war triggered 'regime change' at homeIsrael: Democratic victory raises questions over future of US supportThe Democratic takeover of Congress presents Israel with a set of challenges that extend beyond the immediate impact of the midterm elections, with uncertainty over Trump's Iran strategy, growing criticism of Israel within the Democratic Party and the political calculations surrounding the 2028 presidential race all potentially shaping ties between Washington and Jerusalem.The first concern is how Trump responds to the electoral setback and the political costs of the war with Iran. Analysts quoted by the Jerusalem Post suggest there are two possible paths, either one of renewed diplomatic efforts and concessions to Tehran, or a short but intense military operation aimed at declaring victory and scaling back US involvement.The new balance of power in Congress could pose another challenge. Democratic control of both chambers would give the party greater influence over committee leadership, legislative agendas and congressional scrutiny of Israeli policy, including the war in Gaza and US military assistance.The longer-term question is how the midterm results shape the Democratic Party's approach to Israel ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Candidates who have been openly critical of Israel have seen electoral success with Israeli analysts fearing that politicians such as Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed, alongside a new generation of Democratic lawmakers, could become reference points for candidates seeking support from the party's base. Even a nominee who does not share the most critical positions may face pressure to take a tougher line towards Israel.India: Weakened Trump could push harder for trade dealIndia could face renewed pressure to conclude a trade agreement with Washington as Donald Trump seeks to demonstrate economic and diplomatic gains following his party's defeat in the midterm elections. While Democratic control of Congress could increase scrutiny of his tariff policies, it may do little to change the administration's broader trade approach.An analysis by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) suggests that Trump could turn to executive powers to maintain pressure on trading partners, including India, as both Democrats and Republicans increasingly favour economic nationalism, domestic manufacturing and stronger supply chains.For New Delhi, the immediate concern could be the terms of the proposed bilateral trade agreement. GTRI argues that Trump, facing setbacks in his broader foreign policy efforts involving Russia, China and Iran, could seek a quick trade deal with India to demonstrate American influence.The US could push for greater access to India's agricultural and industrial markets, alongside commitments to purchase $500 billion worth of American goods over five years and align certain security and economic policies with Washington.The proposed arrangement has also raised concerns over the possibility of further US tariffs, including additional duties linked to India's purchases of Russian oil.A Democratic-controlled Congress could increase legislative scrutiny of Trump's tariff policies, but businesses may not see immediate relief from existing duties.Also read: Why a 'lame' duck Donald Trump may push for a quick India-US trade dealCanada: Carney sees opening for trade deal with weakened TrumpThe Republican defeat could give Canada greater leverage in its trade negotiations with Washington, with Canadian PM Mark Carney indicating that the Trump administration had already begun softening some of its demands ahead of the midterm results.Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a Commonwealth leaders' meeting in Antigua on Tuesday, Carney said the White House was “asking less and offering more”, adding that Washington had shifted its position on some of Canada's “red lines”. Canadian federal and provincial officials had been hoping that a Republican setback would strengthen Ottawa's negotiating position, CBC News reported.However, Canada's former ambassador to the US, Kirsten Hillman, cautioned the Carney government against changing course abruptly, saying it should continue constructive discussions if they were moving towards an arrangement acceptable to Canada.The election outcome also raises questions about Trump's ability to advance his domestic agenda. While Democrats will control both chambers of Congress and could pursue legislation on tariffs and other policies, Trump retains significant executive powers and can veto bills passed by lawmakers. A Democratic-led Congress could therefore constrain his agenda through investigations, legislation and scrutiny, but would not automatically be able to reverse his policies.Europe: Democrats may offer a check on Trump, but uncertainty remainsThe Democratic takeover of Congress could give European allies greater room to push back against Trump's approach to Ukraine, Russia and Nato, but it is unlikely to fundamentally alter Washington's foreign policy, with the president retaining considerable authority over diplomacy and military deployments.Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Democrats have broadly supported military assistance to Kyiv and tougher sanctions against Moscow. A Democratic-controlled Congress could make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia or pursue policies that weaken support for Ukraine.However, the electoral setback could also push Trump to focus more heavily on foreign policy, where he retains greater executive authority. This could mean renewed efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, potentially without adequately accounting for Kyiv's position.The implications extend to European security and Nato. The Pentagon is reviewing the US military presence in Europe, with Trump favouring reductions in the number of American troops stationed on the continent. While Democrats have pledged to oppose troop withdrawals, Congress has limited ability to dictate military deployments, which remain largely within the president's authority.With domestic policy increasingly constrained by a Democratic-led Congress, Trump could turn to foreign policy to pursue his priorities and establish his legacy ahead of the 2028 presidential election.South Korea: Caught between the White House and CongressSeoul could face a more complicated relationship with Washington as it navigates a Trump administration and a Democratic-led Congress with potentially different priorities. Former South Korean foreign vice-minister Choi Jong-kun, speaking to a popular Korean current-affairs show, said the country would have to deal separately with the White House and Congress, making diplomacy more challenging.Choi pointed to President Lee Jae-myung’s efforts to secure fuel supplies for nuclear-powered submarines, warning that a Democratic-led Congress could take a stricter position on non-proliferation and create obstacles to the plan. He also questioned whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un would have much incentive to resume high-level talks with Trump if the administration could no longer offer substantive concessions.Economic and defence commitments could also come under greater scrutiny. South Korea has pledged $350 billion in investment in US strategic sectors, including shipbuilding and semiconductors, under an agreement signed last year. The Trump administration could also press Seoul to shoulder more of the cost of stationing US troops in the country, with potential tariff threats and troop reductions adding to the pressure, The Financial News reported.China: Beijing seeks to insulate ties with US from midterm resultsChina has reacted cautiously to the Democratic Party's gains in the US midterm elections, describing the polls as an internal American matter while signalling that it would continue working with Washington to implement agreements reached by the two countries' leaders.“The US midterm elections are a domestic affair,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a media briefing, responding to a question on Beijing's assessment of the results.Mao said China was willing to continue working with the US to uphold and implement the important common understandings reached by president Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump, enhance communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation.She said Beijing was committed to building a constructive relationship of strategic stability with Washington based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, underscoring China's stated preference for continuity in bilateral ties despite changes in the US political landscape.Xi and Trump held two summits this year, including a meeting during the Chinese president's visit to the US from September 23 to 25. The visit marked their second summit since Trump's trip to Beijing in May, with Beijing describing the meetings as a historic milestone aimed at bringing strategic stability to bilateral relations.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union health minister JP Nadda on Wednesday accused the Congress of opposing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists to protect
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union health minister JP Nadda on Wednesday accused the Congress of opposing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists to protect outsiders whose support, he alleged, had helped the party remain in power for a long time.“BJP's Amit Shah favours 'detect, delete and deport'. And what does Congress say? What does INDIA bloc say? They say 'normalise, recognise and formalise',” Nadda said, addressing the 'Loktantra Bachao, Arajakta Hatao' padyatra in Bhopal.The senior BJP leader said the Congress was attempting to undermine constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission, because it was unable to secure public support, PTI reported.Additionally, he alleged that the opposition wanted outsiders to be issued Aadhaar and ration cards and settled in the country so they could become voters.“These people who have come from outside, normalise them. Make Aadhaar cards for them, make ration cards for them, settle them down,” Nadda jibed at Congress.“Tell me, should we detect them or not? Should we deport them or not?” Nadda asked the public, urging it to “delete” the Congress and the INDIA bloc.Nadda accuses Congress of undermining EC credibilityThe BJP leader accused the Congress of attempting to weaken the Election Commission, alleging that the party blamed the poll body whenever it lost elections.“Realising that the electorate is unlikely to grant them any space in the political landscape for the next 20 to 30 years, they have resorted to blaming the Election Commission,” he said.He also accused the Congress of adopting different positions depending on election results, claiming that the party praised Rahul Gandhi when it won in Karnataka and Himachal Pradesh but questioned the Election Commission when it lost.He said Booth Level Officers (BLOs) visiting households to facilitate voter registration reflected the strength of India's electoral system.“In many parts of the world, voters must go to an election office to register their names, whereas in India, a Booth Level Officer (BLO) goes door-to-door to facilitate voter registration, and this is the strength of the Election Commission,” Nadda said.Nadda alleged that the Congress had dismissed elected governments 90 times while in power and questioned its claims of being committed to protecting democracy.Recalling the Emergency imposed in 1975, he claimed that he had been arrested twice by the police while he was a student.Nadda further accused the Congress and the INDIA bloc of attempting to destabilise the country and undermine the credibility of its institutions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Agniveers get 2-year service extension, higher pay: Key changes under revised Agnipath scheme explained
articles.summary: With Diwali just days away, the Union Cabinet has given nearly 20,000 Agniveers a reason to smile, as they now have the opportunity to serve for another
articles.body: With Diwali just days away, the Union Cabinet has given nearly 20,000 Agniveers a reason to smile, as they now have the opportunity to serve for another two years. The Cabinet has made the change just as the initial batch of 24,400 Agniveers was nearing the end of its four-year service term, with as many as 75% of the batch, or 18,300 personnel, set to leave the three armed forces. The first batch of Agniveers from the Navy was set to leave on November 21, the first Air Force batch on December 25 and the Army's batch on December 31.Under the original scheme, those not selected for permanent service would return to civilian life with a Seva Nidhi package, made up of their own contributions and a 30% contribution from the government. The idea was to lower the average age of the armed forces, build a younger fighting force and reduce long-term salary and pension liabilities.What is the Agnipath scheme?The Agnipath scheme was announced on June 14, 2022, with recruitment beginning later that year. It is open to men and women between 17.5 and 21 years of age for posts below the officer cadre in the Army, Navy and Air Force, with recruitment held twice a year. After widespread protests, the government raised the upper age limit to 23, but only for the 2022 cycle due to the pause in recruitment during the Covid-19 pandemic.Agniveers serve for four years, which includes about six months of training followed by three and a half years of actual service. At the end of the tenure, up to 25% of the top performers of a batch were to be absorbed into the permanent cadre, while the remainder would not be eligible for a pension and would leave with a lump sum of around Rs 11 lakh. The government had planned to recruit between 45,000 and 50,000 personnel every year, starting with 46,000 in the first year.The need for AgnipathAt the time of the scheme's implementation, defence personnel expenditure had increased over the previous decade, with the combined share of pay, allowances and pensions rising to as much as 55% of the defence ministry’s expenditure. Meanwhile, the share allocated to equipment acquisition and maintenance had declined by 4%, while research and development accounted for only 3-4%. In 2022-23, pay, allowances and pensions totalled Rs 2,87,040 crore, accounting for 79% of the ministry’s revenue expenditure. The rising pension burden was attributed to salary revisions and the implementation of the One Rank One Pension (OROP) scheme, according to a Delhi-based think tank.Another reason for the recruitment scheme was to create a younger military workforce. The defence ministry estimated that it could bring down the armed forces’ average age from 32 years to 24-26 years. This was in line with recommendations from several expert committees advocating a younger force to meet evolving security challenges. A government comparison of the armed forces of the US, UK, France, Israel, Russia and China placed their average age at around 26-27 years, with engagement periods of two to four years and training lasting three to six months.Agnipath under fireThe announcement of the scheme set off protests in several states, with defence job aspirants objecting to the four-year tenure and the limited scope for permanent recruitment. The lack of long-term job security, the upper age limit of 21 and the recruitment delays during the Covid-19 pandemic added to the discontent among aspirants. The agitation turned violent in many states, with trains and buses set on fire, highways blocked and public property damaged.The protests soon became a political confrontation as well, with the Congress and several regional parties demanding that the scheme be withdrawn, questioning its effect on military careers, operational readiness, cohesion and recruitment. In response to the agitation, the Centre raised the upper age limit to 23 for the 2022 recruitment cycle as a one-time relaxation and announced a 10% reservation for former Agniveers in the central armed police forces and Assam Rifles. Several BJP-ruled states also announced employment preferences for them in their police services, while many private firms said they were looking forward to inducting Agniveers after they completed their four-year term.How the new Agnipath pathway differsThe provision to retain 25% of Agniveers as regular soldiers continues. The remaining 75% will now be offered a second engagement of two years, a decision that follows the armed forces' recommendations after they assessed how the scheme performed in its first four years. At the end of this period, all Agniveers will be offered the chance to enrol as regular soldiers, subject to their willingness and the selection criteria laid down by the services. The extra two years give them more experience before they are considered, but the government has made clear that absorption will not be automatic.Agniveers from the larger pool who choose to continue will be given seniority, though it will be lower than that of the 25% chosen on merit. The scheme itself stays, and its recruitment structure is unchanged. The change is to the exit pathway for the 75%.The second engagement carries higher pay and benefits. According to the briefing by Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani, remuneration will be Rs 43,500 in the first year of the extended period and Rs 47,500 in the second. The government's contribution to the Seva Nidhi package will also go up, with the government increasing its contribution from 30% to 70% of the amount contributed by the individual service member during this extended engagement period, along with other seniority-related benefits.What the review foundThe armed forces' assessment, the CDS stated, found that Agniveers had performed well in physical fitness, motivation, discipline, technological adaptability and skills. The review also pointed to a wider recruitment footprint across the country, with a more transparent and standardised selection process. The order of selection has changed as well, with the written test now held before the physical test, and more avenues will open for women Agniveers. General Subramani said around 25-30% of Agniveers are already deployed in operational areas, underlining that they are performing active military duties.The decision comes against the backdrop of a continuing debate over how the scheme affects unit cohesion and the availability of trained personnel. The government maintains that the revised arrangement will not affect unit cohesion and that the armed forces' recommendations were based on organisational requirements and operational efficiency.The change addresses one of the principal concerns about the original model, which gave regular service to only a quarter of each batch and left most recruits with little chance of a longer career. The remaining Agniveers now have two more years and another shot at permanent enrolment.

articles.title: In 1979, artist Kit Williams buried a jewelled golden hare as a puzzle in his book Masquerade; after being found in 1982 and sold in 1988, it fetched £82,550 at Sotheby’s in 2025
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating tale of Kit Williams' golden hare, a buried treasure from the 1979 puzzle book 'Masquerade', unearthed in 1982 and sold for £82,550 at Sotheby’s in 2025.
articles.body: British artist Kit Williams, in August 1979, buried an 18-carat gold hare decorated with precious stones somewhere in the English countryside. The location of the hare was not revealed through a map or a conventional treasure hunt; instead, it was revealed through a series of intricate riddles that were hidden inside his illustrated children’s book Masquerade. Readers had to examine paintings, verses, numbers and other visual details to get to the correct location of the buried hare. The book became an international publishing sensation after its release. Eventually, the gold hare was unearthed in Ampthill Park, Bedfordshire, in February 1982. More than four decades after the hunt had begun, the jewel returned to Sotheby’s London, where it sold for £82,550 on November 28, 2025.How a children’s picture book became an international treasure huntThe idea behind Masquerade developed from Williams’ interest in making readers follow the illustrations more closely. According to Sotheby’s auction catalogue, publisher Tom Maschler had approached Kit Williams in 1976 about illustrating children’s books. Initially, Williams declined. However, Maschler’s suggestion that he could create something different from the traditional children’s book stayed with him. Instead of just illustrating a story, Williams wanted his readers to analyse his artwork repeatedly and discover the minute details that might otherwise go unnoticed. This eventually became the foundation of Masquerade. The book’s illustrations and accompanying verses contained clues that led to a real object hidden somewhere in Britain.Jonathan Cape published the book in 1979, with the plot of the story focusing on a hare named Jack, who was entrusted by the Moon with a precious jewel to deliver to the Sun. During his journey, the hare lost the jewel. This fictional narrative gave the framework for the real-life treasure hunt in which Williams had created an elaborate golden hare and concealed it in the English countryside. Sotheby's noted that the illustrations consisted of 16 original oil paintings, accompanied by verses and approximately 4,000 words of text. Furthermore, the central puzzle required interpretation of different elements together rather than relying on a single obvious hint.Williams had designed and handcrafted the 18-carat gold hare. He reportedly used techniques like piercing, hammering and riveting for the hare’s decorative chain. The auction house’s description mentions that its body consists of pierced foliate scrollwork, stars and five flower-shaped motifs set with cabochon turquoise. Furthermore, it carries a ruby eye and suspends five small bells which include representations of a mouse, frog and bird. Meanwhile, the necklace includes a crescent moon decorated with mother-of-pearl and a sun mask with citrine eyes. The artist reportedly invested a month in making the jewel, which was valued at approximately £5,000 at the time of burial. The object’s hallmark identifies Williams as the maker, thus making it a distinctive piece of jewellery as well as a centrepiece of a treasure hunt.On the night of August 7, 1979, Williams buried the hare in the presence of television presenter and author Bamber Gascoigne, who acted as his sole witness. The jewel was placed inside a terracotta container which was engraved with a message that identified it as the keeper of the Masquerade treasure. The container was sealed with wax for an additional layer of protection against people attempting to locate the object using metal detectors. Following this, Williams published the book in the same month and began the treasure hunt. The records from the auction house suggest that the first edition of the book sold out within two days. Reports claim that nearly two million treasure seekers from countries like America, Australia, South Africa and Japan attempted to interpret its clues.The discovery in 1982 that did not end the mysteryThe hunt continued for around two and a half years before the golden hare was finally discovered in 1982. The discovery was initially attributed to a man using the name Ken Thomas, though it was later revealed that his real name was Dugald Thompson. According to a report published by The Washington Post on March 15, 1982, Thompson had spent around 18 months following clues from the book but admitted that he had not solved its central riddle. His account involved walking his dog in the park, where the animal led him towards a stone which carried an inscription from Psalm 104. The nearby monument commemorating Catherine of Aragon, the first wife of Henry VIII, helped him connect the location with clues in the book. After several days of digging, he uncovered the terracotta container holding the jewel.This discovery did not establish that Thompson had correctly followed the instructions and solved the puzzle as Williams had originally intended. Mike Barker and John Rousseau, two physics teachers from Manchester, had worked out the book’s master riddle without any outside help. Through their solution, the teachers identified the location, but they had not physically recovered the treasure before Thompson found it. Therefore, the treasure hunt’s apparent conclusion left questions in the wake about whether the person who has been officially credited with discovering the prize had actually deciphered the puzzle.The controversy became more serious in December 1988, when a Sunday Times’ investigation examined Thompson’s identity and his connections to people associated with Williams. A later piece by The Washington Post in 1989 described how Thompson had obtained information about the approximate location through his business associate John Guard, who had a relationship with Williams’ former girlfriend Veronica Robertson. Williams himself expressed disappointment, saying that the revelations tarnished the achievement of his book and the efforts put in by the people who had genuinely tried to solve its mystery.From a £31,900 sale in 1988 to £82,550 sale in 2025The hare entered the auction market in December 1988, when Sotheby’s sold it for £31,900 to an anonymous overseas buyer. The object reportedly remained with the same family for years, largely away from public view. Its whereabouts became known again in 2009, when the BBC documentary The Man Behind the Masquerade brought together Williams and the jewel once again. The owners agreed to lend it for public exhibitions later on.On November 28, 2025, the hare returned to the auction house as part of its Fine Jewels Sale. The auction house had placed an estimate of £15,000 to £20,000 on the piece. articles.title: Zac Brown founded Camp Southern Ground in Georgia in 2011; 15 years later, its 11.5-acre organic farm helps feed campers while programmes support children, veterans and military families
articles.summary: When Zac Brown founded Camp Southern Ground in Georgia in 2011, he wanted to create more than a summer camp.
articles.body: When Zac Brown founded Camp Southern Ground in Georgia in 2011, he wanted to create more than a summer camp. He wanted a place where children, veterans and military families could step away from daily pressures, build confidence, form friendships and find a sense of purpose. Fifteen years later, that vision has grown into a 400-acre campus in Fayetteville with an 11.5-acre USDA Certified Organic farm, sustainability-focused buildings and programmes designed to serve people at different stages of life, as per Camp Southern Ground's website.The organisation marked its fifteenth anniversary in June 2026, describing the milestone as a celebration of the thousands of children, veterans and military families who have found belonging, connection and opportunity there. Its work now extends well beyond campfires and outdoor activities. Camp Southern Ground offers inclusive summer programming for children, free programmes for veterans, and family-focused support for those whose lives have been shaped by military service.At the heart of the campus is a practical idea: good food, time outdoors and meaningful connection can help people grow. The farm supplies three meals a day for campers and veterans, while the wider organisation uses music, recreation, education and peer support to help participants build skills that last long after they leave Georgia. Read more about it here:A camp built around inclusionCamp Southern Ground was created to welcome children from many backgrounds and with many different needs. Its summer camp model focuses on belonging, social-emotional learning and character development, an approach that earned national recognition when the National Summer Learning Association awarded the organisation its Summer Learning Legacy Award in February 2026.The camp has also received accreditation from the National Inclusion Project, a recognition that reflects its commitment to serving children of different backgrounds and abilities. For families, that matters because a camp experience is only meaningful if every child can take part fully rather than being placed on the edge of the activity.Camp Southern Ground has continued to develop that inclusive approach through partnerships and new facilities. In 2025, the Peachtree City Rotary Club helped create a sensory path on campus, giving campers another way to explore, recharge and connect with nature. The organisation has also worked with Generation WE to use storytelling and art to help young people express themselves and recognise the value of their own experiences.The farm that feeds the campusThe 11.5-acre USDA Certified Organic farm is one of the most visible parts of Camp Southern Ground’s mission. It helps supply three meals a day for campers and veterans, with chef-prepared meals following a gluten-free, allergen-free and anti-inflammatory diet. The farm is not simply a food source. It is also a classroom. Campers can spend time in a one-acre demonstration garden, prepare a dish with their own hands and see where their meals begin before they reach the dining hall. According to the organisation, 71 percent of campers tried a new food last year, a sign that hands-on exposure can make healthy eating feel less intimidating.Camp Southern Ground says reconnecting people with the origins of their food helps them understand food sources, develop healthier habits and consider the environmental impact of how food is grown and transported. In that sense, the farm supports both personal wellbeing and a broader lesson in sustainability.Sustainability is part of the designThe organisation’s environmental commitments extend beyond the organic farm. Its campus includes LEED-certified buildings designed to combine modern technology, architecture and sustainability. Materials such as zinc siding, which the organisation says is 100 percent recyclable, are intended to help the buildings last for decades.The campus also uses Dedicated Outdoor Air Systems alongside a geothermal ground loop system, which draws on groundwater from strategically placed wells to help condition air before it enters buildings. A five-acre solar field is intended to allow the camp to operate off the power grid during the day and possibly overnight.Those systems are paired with smaller practical measures, including LED and low-voltage lighting, computer-managed lighting systems and occupancy sensors that prevent energy waste in empty spaces. The organisation also says it uses hypoallergenic green seal cleaning products and recyclable materials to protect guests and reduce environmental impact.Support for veterans and military familiesWhile the farm and summer camp are central to the campus, Camp Southern Ground’s work with veterans has become a major part of its identity. Its Warrior Programmes are offered free of charge to veterans nationwide and are designed to help service members and their families find purpose, connection and growth after military service.One of the organisation’s best-known offerings is Warrior PATHH, a programme focused on post-traumatic growth. The camp says it helps veterans navigate life after service by providing community, understanding and practical tools for recovery and personal development.The organisation also brings military families together through programmes such as its work with TAPS. In March 2025, 16 Gold Star families gathered at Camp Southern Ground for a weekend focused on healing, connection and joy. The camp has also continued its partnership with Camp Corral, which provides summer camp experiences for children of wounded, ill and fallen military heroes.Music as a bridgeMusic remains closely tied to the camp’s identity, partly because of Brown’s background as the founder of Zac Brown Band. The organisation’s Warrior Song programme brings veteran singer-songwriters together for several days of collaboration, mentorship and creative development.In 2025, the fourth annual Warrior Song brought together veteran artists for intensive songwriting sessions and guidance from industry professionals. The camp described the programme as a way to help participants develop creatively while also building connection with others who understand the transition from military service.Music also plays a public role in fundraising and awareness. Camp Southern Ground hosted its inaugural Unsung Hero LIVE benefit concert in November 2025, followed by a second Unsung Hero event in 2026, headlined by Emily Ann Roberts. The organisation says the concerts celebrate veterans, music and the stories that inspire people, with proceeds supporting its Warrior Programmes.Fifteen years of growthCamp Southern Ground’s fifteenth year has included both reflection and expansion. The organisation reported that 2025 was a year of growth, with more children, veterans and military families served than ever before, along with new moments of connection, fresh food grown on campus and expanded campus resources.Leadership has also changed. Longtime chief executive Mike Dobbs retired after a decade in the role, and the board named Michael Caimona, a Navy veteran and experienced executive, as the organisation’s next CEO beginning in May 2026. The organisation says his background reflects a continued commitment to the veteran community.For Brown, the camp’s longevity is the clearest evidence that its original idea still matters. What began as one founder’s vision has become a working farm, a summer camp, a veteran support centre and a gathering place for families. Fifteen years later, Camp Southern Ground continues to show that a meal grown on site, a shared campfire and a community that understands your experience can be powerful forms of care.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1995, Washington rebuilt a road near Ilwaco on shredded tyres; by January 1996 the surface reached 165°F from inside, and in 1997 federal guidelines capped some such fills at 3 m
articles.summary: Discover the 1995 Washington Road project that utilized shredded tyres, leading to a severe environmental incident and prompting new engineering guidelines for safer construction practices.
articles.body: An experiment designated to reuse scrap tyres for construction material resulted in an accident in southwestern Washington during the mid 1990s. A group of engineers seeking a solution for the repair of a damaged road from the landslide used crushed tyres instead of soil and rocks to fill the void spaces. This method addressed two growing problems at the same time, namely disposing of scrap materials and helping restore roads. Unfortunately, shortly after the completion of the project, cracks appeared, steam was released, and heat was generated. What followed was an environmental incident involving burning tyres and the release of an oil-like substance in a coastal wetland.According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, a landslide took place in December 1994 on the State Route 100 Loop that is located near Ilwako, Washington. Rebuilding was done in the summer of 1995, when tire chips ranging from 2 to 6 inches in size were used as fillers for the asphalt. The road opened on November 3, 1995, although cracks began appearing in late December. Then, on 5th January 1996, the surface of the road recorded a temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit.Why shredded tyres were usedThe initial decision was based on engineering advantages. A huge amount of scrap tyres was being stored in different parts of the United States because disposal was a problem. Therefore, the tyres could be shredded into smaller pieces to be used in civil engineering projects where lightweight filling material was required. In the case of Illwako, the tyres were being used to reconstruct a part of the road that was affected by unstable soil conditions. The lightweight of the tyres made them ideal for the reconstruction of the slope without putting additional pressure on the soil.Research published in the Journal of Geotechnical and Geoenvironmental Engineering reviewed the use of tyre chips for highway embankments. The study recognised the possibility of utility of tyre chips as a lightweight construction material if used within suitable engineering practice. During that period, this method of recycling tyres seemed promising, both for infrastructure purposes as well as from a waste management point of view. But this approach had one major drawback, which became evident throughout the project at Illwako.Heat, smoke and an unexpected environmental emergencyCracks first appeared in road surfaces in December 1995. In January 1996, heat was venting through the crack holes. By the third of January 1996, the temperature had risen up to 165° F. Furthermore, monitoring of air quality and underground water seepage started on 17 January 1996. The situation became more severe in March 1996, when an oil-like substance began seeping out of the ground with groundwater. According to NOAA, it was identified as pyrolytic oil resulting from thermal decomposition of rubber. Between 300 and 400 gallons of the substance had seeped from the hill before the leak was controlled on 14 March.The Baker Bay Coastal wetlands containing fish, birds, and other wildlife were endangered as a result of the incident. About gallons of oil had seeped out into the intertidal areas, therefore affecting 300 to 350 square feet of shoreline. Contaminant barriers, absorbent material, and copper dams were used to contain the contamination. Additionally, officials tried to minimise oxygen supply to the embankment. The actual components responsible for the heating could not be ascertained. It was thought that factors like oxidation, humidity, steel belt exposure, and biological activity could have contributed to the cause.New engineering guidelines followed the incidentThe case was not a singular event. In 1995, there were three projects involving shredded tyres in the US that had heating difficulties, which involved two projects in Washington State and one project in Colorado. This prompted engineers and federal transportation authorities to reconsider the use of recycled tyres in large construction projects. In July 1997, the Federal Highway Administration provided interim design guidelines for reducing internal heat generated by tyre shred fills. They involved more regulation of the thickness of tyres used in the process, minimising the exposure of steel and avoiding high levels of moisture and air penetration.The guidelines gave a maximum allowable thickness of 3 m for some uses of tyre-derived aggregate fills. It was clear that, for material reuse to be effective in infrastructure development, the characteristics of the material had to be taken into account. Proper design of the use of tyre shred could make them useful engineering materials. Thus, the Ilwaco experience was an eye-opener for the experimentalists.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Celina Poon, the 19-year-old Boston student who helped more than 300 young people engage with civic life and organized an arts fair bringing together 12 local artists and community groups
articles.summary: Celina Poon spent her early childhood in Boston without learning much about local government or how to get involved in her community.
articles.body: Celina Poon spent her early childhood in Boston without learning much about local government or how to get involved in her community. Growing up in an immigrant family, she often saw public institutions as distant and difficult to understand. She only learned about civic education later in her youth. That experience inspired the 19-year-old student to help other young people in her hometown become more involved in their communities. As an intern with the Commonwealth Seminar, a Massachusetts organization that works to make public life more accessible, Poon led projects that helped more than 300 young people learn about local government and community action. Her efforts earned national recognition from Youth Service America, which named her an Everyday Young Hero in October 2026. The award recognizes young leaders across the United States who use volunteer work and community service to address local needs.Opening doors for young citizensThe Commonwealth Seminar works to make state and local government easier to understand, especially for communities that have often been left out of public discussions. When Poon joined the organization as an intern, she became responsible for planning its youth conference. She created the educational program, arranged guest speakers, and organized workshops for teenagers and young adults who had little experience with local government and public policy. According to profiles published by Youth Service America, her program showed participants how to turn everyday problems in their neighborhoods into organized efforts to bring about change. Poon pointed out that many young people and immigrant families want to make their neighborhoods better but do not know where to begin. Without a clear understanding of how local government works or how to contact lawmakers, many residents remain disconnected from decisions that affect their daily lives. Her conference aimed to make learning about government more practical. Instead of focusing only on classroom lessons, she gave participants useful skills. These included taking part in public meetings, contacting local representatives, and organizing efforts to address neighborhood problems.Blending community arts with public lifeAlong with planning the conference, Poon created the Arts and Culture Fair. The event was designed to bring together creative activities and community involvement. It featured 12 local artists and community organizations in Boston, showing how art projects can help shape neighborhood identity and support social change. The fair gave local artists a chance to display work about cultural history, public spaces, and equal opportunities. At the same time, local non-profit organizations set up interactive booths where visitors could learn about their work and community programs. By bringing local art and community services together, Poon wanted to make civic participation feel welcoming and easy to understand rather than complicated or formal. The event gave residents a relaxed place to discuss public policy, community identity, and changes to their neighborhoods. Youth Service America organizers noted that Poon's approach showed how creative activities outside traditional government settings can encourage more people to take part in public life. This was especially important for young people who might not normally attend town hall meetings or public hearings.Applying architecture to community preservationPoon's work in community organizing also connects with her studies. She is currently a second-year Bachelor of Architecture student at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Her studies explore how the design of buildings and public spaces can affect the way people connect with one another. Her academic interests include protecting older neighborhoods, preserving historic buildings, and creating public spaces that everyone can access. According to her profile on Youth Service America's website, Poon hopes to use her design skills to protect places that hold cultural importance for longtime residents. She is particularly interested in everyday public spaces and historic buildings that may be demolished or neglected during urban redevelopment. Poon believes that well-designed public buildings and spaces can help communities maintain trust, preserve their history, and stay connected. Her future plans include combining the restoration of historic buildings with community outreach. She wants to make sure longtime residents have a direct say in how their neighborhoods change over time. By bringing together architecture and the civic education projects she developed in Boston, Poon hopes to help communities protect their local history while creating welcoming public spaces for future generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1983, Minnesota paved two airport roads with asphalt mixed with sewage-sludge ash; by 1990, it was on three highways, and a federal review found no visible difference
articles.summary: This article explores Minnesota's innovative approach of utilizing sewage sludge ash in asphalt for road construction, highlighting its benefits, environmental considerations, and the results of federal evaluations.
articles.body: A unique experiment in constructing roads in Minnesota illustrated how the material that was left over from the sewage treatment process could be recycled as well as used for building purposes. The engineers did not want to discard all of the ash from sewage-sludge incineration, but instead wanted to use it in asphalt road construction. The utilisation of this material would help solve two problems: the growing quantity of waste from the sewage treatment plants and the utilisation of materials in road construction.According to the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), Minnesota started incorporating ash from sewage sludge into asphalt in 1983, when two bypass roads at the Minneapolis–St. Paul International Airport were constructed using asphalt that contained 2% or 3% ash. Additional demonstration projects were undertaken in 1989 and 1990 and included the construction of the I-94 bridge overpass as well as segments of TH–47 in Ramsay and TH-97 in Forest Lake Township.Turning sewage waste into rad building materialSewage sludge is the residue left after solids are separated from wastewater during treatment. Incineration of the sewage sludge leads to the formation of ash residue, which needs proper handling. The Metropolitan Base Control Commission of Minnesota, currently operating under the Environmental Services of Metropolitan Council, has initiated a study on the use of this residue in construction rather than disposal. The study was focused on the use of sewage sludge ash as mineral fillers in hot mix asphalt (HMA). Mineral fillers are useful for occupying spaces between aggregate particles in HMA. Therefore, the finely divided nature of the ash made it a suitable replacement for materials like stone dust and hydrated lime.Initial investigation by the Minnesota Department of Transportation examined the physical properties of the ash and its behaviour in asphalt mixtures. Research published in Construction and Building Materials has also studied the use of sewage sludge ash as a substitute for regular mineral failure in asphalt pavement mixtures, considering aspects like stability, density, and air void content. The Minnesota experiment was especially noteworthy since no special road construction methods had to be developed. The ash could be incorporated into regular asphalt mixers without any need for a new method of mixing, laying, or compacting the material.From airport bypass roads to state highwaysField demonstrations were conducted in 1983 at Minnesota Saint Paul International Airport. Two bypass roads utilised sludge ash as a constituent of pavement layers such as base binder and wearing courses. These mixtures used either 2% or 3% ash, depending on the test, and the I–94 bridge overpass project used a wearing course in 1989 and 1992. A segment of TH-47 in Ramsay was made with a 2% ash content in the levelling and wearing courses, while TH-97 in Forest Lake Township was constructed with a 2% ash content in its base, binder, and wearing courses. These projects provide possibilities for testing this material in real traffic and weather conditions, unlike a laboratory setting. FHWA reported that there was no apparent difference between sections with sewage sludge ash and conventional sections. It is quite promising, but this does not mean that these pavements perform equally well across all settings.What the federal review revealedThe FHWA Technical Assessment included more detail on how sewage sludge ash can be used in asphalt mixtures. It is pointed out that the properties of a mixture that includes 2 to 5% ash, in relation to the weight of aggregate, can be equal to those of mineral filler. It was suggested that the amount of ash should be limited to 5% in relation to the aggregate weight and 3% in case of wearing course. The incinerated ash might also have some environmental impacts, but considering this, the team has suggested using a minimal amount.However, the organisation indicated that, despite the successes of sewage sludge, it has not yet been accepted for broader commercial use in the USA. Such implementation requires specific material requirements, mix design standards, and environmental monitoring. Nevertheless, an experiment conducted by the state of Minnesota provided an available example of recycling waste in transport infrastructure.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Birla proposes digital audit platform for state legislatures, calls for timely action on PAC reports
articles.summary: Om Birla proposes a common digital audit monitoring platform for state PACs, urging timely action on CAG reports, enforceable timelines and Centre-state coordination.
articles.body: Thiruvananthapuram: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has proposed a common digital audit monitoring platform for state legislatures, similar to the platform available to parliamentary committees, to facilitate systematic monitoring of audit observations and ensure the timely examination and disposal of audit reports.Speaking at the valedictory of the two-day Conference of Chairpersons of Public Accounts Committees (PAC) of Parliament of India and States/UTs Legislatures on Wednesday, Birla said the platform would strengthen follow-up mechanisms and improve the monitoring of audit findings.Referring to Lok Sabha PAC chairperson P C Venugopal’s suggestions, Birla called for Parliament and state legislatures to jointly develop a system for continuous audit scrutiny and timely disposal of reports.He said a coordinated institutional mechanism would promote synergy and experience-sharing and strengthen PACs nationwide.Birla said CAG audit observations must lead to corrective action and tangible improvements in administration.The executive, he said, must accord due importance to the recommendations of the committees and ensure timely implementation.Birla said rising public investment in sectors including education, healthcare, infrastructure, social welfare and rural development made the prudent use of public funds increasingly important.Venugopal said the conference proposed enforceable timelines for govts to respond to committee recommendations and called for at least one PAC report to be discussed annually in Parliament and state legislatures.He also called for closer Centre-state coordination in scrutinising centrally sponsored schemes and proposed at least one annual meeting of Union and state PACs on the schemes.Venugopal said the previous Parliament’s PAC found that pre- and post-matric scholarships for SC students had been delayed for seven years, with neither Centre nor the states aware of the amount disbursed.Through the Keralam Resolution, the conference called for a digital portal to facilitate peer learning and sharing of best practices among PACs, along with standard timelines for action taken notes and digital audit-monitoring systems such as audit para monitoring system.State and Union territory PACs were urged to meet at least three times a month, form sub-committees to clear pending audit observations and work closely with the CAG’s office to use forensic tools to identify high-risk areas requiring legislative oversight.Stay updated with the latest Thiruvananthapuram articles.body: Kolkata: Supreme Court on Wednesday directed Md Nazibuddin Mondal alias Tulu Mondal — accused in the Birbhum illegal sand mining case — to return to India from Dubai by Nov 17 to face questioning, granting him protection from arrest for three weeks from the date of his arrival. articles.title: State launches digital salary advance scheme for govt employees
articles.summary: West Bengal launches digital Salary Advance Scheme for govt staff, offering short-term and multi-month advances plus higher Rs 1.2 lakh two-wheeler loan cap.
articles.body: Kolkata: State govt employees can now access salary advances to meet emergency needs, including medical expenses, children’s education and unforeseen household expenditures, under a new scheme introduced by the finance department.A notification has been issued introducing West Bengal Salary Advance Scheme, which provides a digital platform for employees to avail themselves of short-term and multi-month salary advances. The initiative aims to offer institutional financial assistance and reduce dependence on high-interest loans from external sources. It will cover regular govt employees across Groups A to D and equivalent categories.The scheme has two components — short-term and multi-month advances. Under the short-term facility, employees can avail themselves of up to 50% of their monthly salary entitlement to meet urgent financial requirements. The amount must be repaid within the same or immediately succeeding salary cycle, subject to a maximum of 60 days, as specified in the memorandum of understanding (MoU) or platform terms. No interest, processing fee, platform fee or convenience fee will be charged if repayment is made within the stipulated period.A transaction fee of up to 1% may be imposed if delays in providing information are attributable to the employee. No additional charge will apply if the delay is caused by the govt department or drawing and disbursing officer (DDO).The multi-month facility is intended for larger, planned expenditures, allowing repayment in instalments over two to 60 months. The tenure cannot extend beyond the employee’s retirement date. The eligible amount will depend on the lender’s risk assessment and Reserve Bank of India guidelines. It may go up to 30 times monthly gross salary, with the monthly EMI capped at 50% of gross salary.Employees will receive advance statements detailing applicable interest rates and charges, in accordance with digital lending guidelines. Monthly instalments will be deducted directly from salaries after obtaining digital consent. Outstanding dues may also be adjusted against final settlement benefits in case of resignation or retirement.Separately, state govt has raised the financial ceiling for advances to purchase motorcycles, scooters and electric two-wheelers. Employees can now avail themselves of up to Rs 1.20 lakh.
